doc.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

chapter: On the road with Spivak and Sauter-Finegan
title: Dances, colleges and the Spivak trombone section
summary: Describes ballroom and college dance work, Kai Winding's college circuit, and learning from Vinnie Forchetti after replacing Leon Cox.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Oh yeah. Bands in those days were playing public dances, which you don’t see anymore, in a ballroom in Indiana or something like that, that all the bands went through, Lake Compounce, Connecticut, all the bands went through, and you’d play at officers clubs, NCO clubs in the service, and the big thing too bands did in those days, yeah, I remember that in this band, is you’d go into a college and you would play a dance on Friday night, a concert on Saturday afternoon and a dance Saturday night. So that was like a long weekend in a college. And colleges used to hired bands that way. As a matter of fact Kai Winding got wised up. Kai Winding was a very good businessman. He decided he was going to take his trombone band and compete with the big bands. So he started getting a lot of that work after he decided he didn’t want to play the jazz clubs anymore. So he was jumping around playing these colleges, not all over the country but from here to the Mississippi River, generally that’s where most of the business was. One time with Spivak we ended up in Texas I remember for like — and everything was done with a bus, not with Kai Winding but with Charlie Spivak it was a bus — anyways I came out of the service and I mean I could talk for a long, long time on the experience in Charlie Spivak’s band and how I learned. You know I was young and I grew up with Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker and everything else. Most of the guys in the band were a little older than that, right? So when I did get — I took Leon Cox’s place as a matter of fact, I don’t know if you know that name, but he was the guy that played the very, very famous trombone solo on Gene Krupa’s record of “Lover.” It’s a very unusual solo. And

so when I moved up from third trombone to second trombone, when he left — I never did play first trombone in that band — I learned a lot from Vinnie Forchetti, who was playing first trombone in that band for the last part of the time I was on it. I learned a lot from him. But I had one guy in back of me who loved me dearly, he was kind of a jokester, his name was Buddy Hanna and everything else, and he played kind of like Sweets Edison you know and stuff like that. But he’d yell down at me and says, “Stop playing that Chinese music.” I was hearing things bebop. And although I knew very little about harmony, I was doing everything by ear and everything else, that’s what was coming out. That was my roots you see.
